t1.text: Moving an order, and moving it back

nA.text:
THE MOVE THAT NEEDS ONE FACT

Only two of the five moves need anything from you, and each needs exactly one thing: who is carrying it, and what came in short. So the sheet asks one question and stops — 480px, four parts, two buttons.

No stage track across the top: you know where the order is. The pair in the foot says where it is going.

nB.text:
STEPPING BACK

There is no way back on the board today. `prev` is written and complete — it retires the driver, clears the carrier note, resets the pick and re-offers it — and nothing anywhere renders it.

The sheet names what the step back undoes, in one sentence, because that is the part that costs somebody work.

nC.text:
CANCEL, OUT OF THE ALERT BOX

Three moves ask through the browser's own confirm(): cancel an order, close a whole run, invoice everything delivered. An OS alert with \n\n in it, on a screen that has its own dialog.

The consequence the code already works out — which goods are on the shelf and whose bill is raised — belongs on the sheet, in the app's own type.

nD.text:
WHAT REPLACES MOST OF THE ASKING

A move that needs nothing should not ask. It happens on the tap, and for fifteen seconds it can be taken back.

This is the reason the sheets can stay small: only a move that needs a fact, or that cannot be undone, gets one.

nE.text:
THE RULE UNDER ALL OF IT

Today you can press "Move on" and have nothing happen but a toast in the corner. That is what "not working" looks like from the outside.

A button that would refuse should not be that button. It should be the thing standing in the way.

nF.text:
THE SAME SHEET, ONE-HANDED

820px is a switch, not a reflow: it comes up from the foot, taps are 48px, and the two buttons are the width of the screen.

One question is one question in either hand.
